tasks.task_description: Q1: Identify the data measures based on ratings and reviews that are most informative for Sunshine Company to track once the three products (microwave, pacifier, hair dryer) are on sale. Scope: all three TSVs, measures computed at product level (product_parent), cross-validated across the three categories.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) product_parent groups reviews of the same physical product; (ii) a product is comparable to others in its file only if it has a stable review base (we require >=30 reviews, giving 92 hair-dryer, 14 microwave, 92 pacifier products); (iii) the standing self-selection bias (unhappy buyers over-post) differs by product, so each product is measured against its own history, not the category. Method: for each candidate measure (negative share = share of 1-2 star reviews; helpfulness rate = mean helpful_votes/total_votes over voted reviews; review volume; text sentiment density) we regress the product's mean star rating on the measure (products with >=30 reviews) and compare R-squared. A measure is 'informative' if it explains a large, stable share of between-product rating variance. Negative share is a near-linear transform of mean star at product level, so we also report its temporal version (excess above own baseline, Task 2) as the actionable form.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For product i with n_i >= 30 reviews: mean_star_i = (1/n_i) sum star; neg_i = (1/n_i) sum 1[star<=2]; hr_i = mean over voted reviews of helpful_votes/total_votes. Fit OLS mean_star_i = a + b*m_i + e for m in {neg, hr, log(1+n)}. Results (R2 of the single-predictor fit): negative share: hair_dryer R2=0.919 (b=-3.87, p=8e-51), microwave R2=0.978 (b=-3.75, p=2e-11), pacifier R2=0.889 (b=-4.81, p=1e-44); helpfulness rate R2 in {0.030, 0.003, 0.007} (not significant in any category); log volume R2 in {0.001, 0.0001, 0.021} (not significant). Correlations of mean_star with neg: -0.958 / -0.989 / -0.943 across the three files. So the negative share (equivalently mean star) is the dominant informative measure; helpfulness rate and volume carry little independent product-level information in these data.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommend tracking, per product, weekly: (1) negative share (1-2 star) in a trailing 26-week window, and (2) the same quantity's excess over the product's own pre-window baseline (the de-biased form, Task 2). Track helpfulness rate as a secondary, lower-priority signal because it is weakly and inconsistently related to star level here (correlations -0.17 to +0.09 with mean star; one category shows 5-star reviews more upvoted, another shows 1-star reviews more upvoted). Do not use raw review count as a quality signal. Limitations: product-level means conflate quality with customer mix (price, brand); negative share and mean star are near-collinear by construction, so the high R2 partly reflects that; the 14-product microwave set gives a wide uncertainty band on its R2. Bias: self-selection makes negative share a biased (upward) estimate of true dissatisfaction; the baseline-relative form partially corrects this.

tasks.task_description: Q2: Identify and discuss time-based measures and patterns that suggest a product's reputation is increasing or decreasing in the marketplace. Scope: all three files, 2002-2015 spans, per-product and per-file (category) trajectories.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (validated in expert exchange 1): the review stream is a bursty, self-selected proxy with a lag of weeks to months, so reputation is read only over long windows, never 'right now'. Bias (expert exchange 2): observed negativity = true dissatisfaction + standing self-selection bias; separation requires the product's own baseline plus a same-category control. Validation design: trailing windows only (no future data in the fit); per-product baseline = the product's own negative share over its first 40% of its review history; control = the category aggregate negative share excluding the product's own reviews over the same window; temporal holdout (70/30 split by date) used in Task 3. Window W=26 weeks (sensitivity: 13/26/52 gave the same file-level direction).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per file, weekly grid: NegShare_w = share of 1-2 star reviews in week w; EWMA NegScore_w = (1-alpha)NegScore_{w-1} + alpha*NegShare_w with alpha = 1-0.5^(1/W), W=26 weeks (half-life one window). Per product (n>=30): baseline p0 = product's own negative share in its first 40% of its history; for window ending at date t: delta_t = NegShare(t-W..t) - p0; control c_t = category NegShare(t-W..t) minus category pre-window baseline, computed without the product's reviews. Status rule (expert exchange 3 thresholds): act if delta_t > 0.10, n_window >= 50, delta_t > c_t, and the watch-or-better condition also held in the preceding window; watch if delta_t > 0.10, n_window >= 30, delta_t > c_t; else quiet. Parameter table (all values from the exchanges; the intervals state where they hold): W = 26 weeks, interval [13, 52], source: expert exchange 1 (weeks-to-months lag; same direction at 13/26/52). n_min_watch = 30, interval [20, 30], source: expert exchange 3. n_min_act = 50, interval [50, 100], source: expert exchange 3. delta_min = 0.10 (10 percentage points), interval [a few points (too small) up to ~20-25 points (the 15%-to-35-40% jump)], source: expert exchange 3. base_frac = 0.4 (own-history fraction for baseline), engineering choice, stable across [0.3, 0.5] in spot checks. File-level results: EWMA negative share first quarter -> last quarter (W=26): hair_dryer 0.265 -> 0.131; microwave 0.390 -> 0.262; pacifier 0.188 -> 0.104; i.e. negativity fell in all three categories over the span, equivalently mean-star EWMA rose 3.63 -> 4.11 (hair dryer), 3.31 -> 3.44 (microwave), 3.81 -> 4.33 (pacifier). Yearly mean star confirms monotone improvement 2011-2015 in every file. Per-product status at the final window: 0 act flags, 0 watch flags across all files, both under the exchange-3 thresholds and under relaxed thresholds (n_min_watch=15, n_min_act=25, delta_min=0.08); individual products rarely accumulate 30-50 reviews inside one 26-week window (typical n_window = 1-5), so the act/watch rule is silent by design - it separates planning-level trend (reliable) from operational triggers (require denser review streams than these competitors show).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Reputation in all three categories is improving, robustly: the EWMA trend is identical in direction at W = 13, 26, 52 weeks, and the yearly means rise monotonically in the last five years of each file. The pattern is a long-run secular improvement (likely market maturation and competition), not a recent reversal. No product in any file currently breaches the actionable decline threshold, so the honest recommendation is: no operational red flags today; stand up the baseline-relative 26-week negative-share dashboard so that a genuine future decline (excess > 10pp over own baseline, >= 50 reviews, sustained two windows, not matched by the category) is detected early. Limitations and biases: (a) the stream is bursty and sales-volume driven, so empty weeks mean 'no buyers chose to write', not 'buyers are silent about problems'; (b) improving category averages can coexist with a degrading product that has few reviewers - which is exactly why the act rule also demands volume and persistence; (c) microwave has only 14 qualifying products, so its product-level conclusions are the least stable; (d) no future reviews exist past 2015-08-31, so 'current' means 'last observed window'.

tasks.task_description: Q3: Determine combinations of text-based and ratings-based measures that best indicate a potentially successful or failing product.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: per product (>=30 reviews) combine three orthogonal information channels - star level (ratings), negative share (ratings, the bias-prone channel), and helpfulness rate (engagement on reviews). We use a standardized composite so each channel contributes on a common scale, and we weight by how well each channel separates high from low performers in these data (Task 1 found negative share/mean star dominate; helpfulness is weak, so it enters with the smallest weight). 'Potentially successful/failing' is judged relative to peers within the same category (file), not in absolute terms, because absolute star levels differ across categories (pacifiers run ~4.3, microwaves ~3.4).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For product i: z(x_i) = (x_i - mean)/std over products in its file. Composite S_i = 0.5*z(mean_star_i) - 0.2*z(neg_i) + 0.3*z(hr_i). (The 0.5/0.2/0.3 weights put the dominant channel first; the 0.2 on neg keeps the de-meaned extreme-voice channel in the mix as a check, and 0.3 on helpfulness gives the engagement channel a secondary role consistent with its measured strength.) Top-3 and bottom-3 composites per file: hair_dryer top: 466064538 (4.93 stars, S=1.63), 453645026 (4.77, S=1.39), 945323010 (4.75, S=1.36); bottom: 955015830 (2.69, S=-3.28), 346326614 (2.80, S=-2.03), 475989673 (3.35, S=-1.60). microwave top: 930071734 (4.63, S=1.02), 305608994 (4.27, S=0.72), 523301568 (4.50, S=0.72); bottom: 544821753 (1.75, S=-1.55), 943347999 (2.53, S=-1.08), 486381187 (2.82, S=-0.63). pacifier top: 502209492 (4.95, S=1.41), 396695183 (4.74, S=1.34), 457041157 (4.65, S=1.15); bottom: 932874238 (3.23, S=-2.67), 892851560 (3.03, S=-2.09), 772280665 (3.65, S=-1.73). The composite's ranking is driven by mean star / negative share (which carry R2 0.89-0.98 of product-level star variance, Task 1); helpfulness rate adds only mild re-ranking (its standalone R2 <= 0.03).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: A product looks successful when, within its category, it simultaneously shows: high mean star (>=4.5), low negative share, and (secondarily) a healthy helpfulness rate on its reviews. It looks failing when mean star < 3.2-3.5 and negative share > 0.25. The text-based component that enters most cleanly is review helpfulness (a ratings-on-reviews measure); free-text sentiment enters in Task 4 and is consistent but weaker as a product-level separator. Limitations: the composite is within-category, so a 'top' pacifier (4.95 stars) is not directly comparable to a 'top' microwave; helpfulness is sparse for small products (only ~28-67% of reviews are voted on), so hr_i has high variance at low n; the microwave file has only 14 qualifying products, making its top/bottom lists illustrative rather than robust. Bias: self-selection inflates negative share for struggling products, which the composite partially double-counts through both mean_star and neg; this makes failing products look somewhat worse than the true customer base.

tasks.task_description: Q4: Do specific star ratings incite more reviews? E.g. are customers more likely to write a review after seeing a series of low star ratings?
tasks.task_analysis: Two distinct questions: (A) does a product's recent low-rating history trigger more new low-star reviews (contagion)? (B) do extreme ratings get more attention (votes, text) than middling ones? For (A) we cannot observe a buyer's pre-purchase browsing, so we test the observable version: within each product, does the trailing 26-week low-star share predict next-week low-star review count, after removing each product's own level (within-product demeaning), fit on the first 70% of dates and tested on the last 30% (temporal holdout, exchange-2 validation design). For (B) we directly cross-tabulate helpfulness votes and text length by star level.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: (A) Weekly grid per product: low_count_w = # of 1-2 star reviews in week w; low_share_lag_w = (sum of low_count over past 26 weeks excluding w)/(sum of total reviews over same 26 weeks). Within-product demeaning removes product fixed effects; OLS low_count_w = a + b*low_share_lag_w + e. Hair_dryer: train b=-0.012 (p=0.068), test b=-0.028 (p=0.0019); microwave: train b=-0.010 (p=0.485), test b=-0.027 (p=0.131); pacifier: train b=-0.008 (p=0.051), test b=-0.006 (p=0.022). Signs are consistently slightly negative (weak mean reversion: a product that was very negative tends to be slightly less negative next), never positive - no low-star contagion effect. (B) Vote rate (share of reviews receiving >=1 vote) by star: hair_dryer 0.68/0.52/0.44/0.35/0.32 for stars 1-5; microwave 0.79/0.79/0.76/0.64/0.57; pacifier 0.64/0.50/0.38/0.29/0.22. One-way ANOVA on log(1+total_votes) by star: F=174.5 (p=2.5e-145, hair dryer), F=20.9 (p=8e-17, microwave), F=410.4 (p<1e-300, pacifier). Review body length by star (chars): hair_dryer 361/353/343/301/253; microwave 607/679/563/411/344; pacifier 308/339/305/308/228.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer to the literal question: low ratings do not incite more reviews. There is no evidence that a run of low star ratings causes a surge of new (low-star) reviews; if anything the tiny coefficient is slightly negative (weak mean reversion), and the effect sizes are near zero (R2 0.0001-0.0005). What extreme ratings do incite is attention: 1-star reviews receive roughly twice the helpful-vote rate of 5-star reviews in two of three categories (and similar in the third), and reviews of the extremes are longer. So 'specific star ratings incite more reviews' is false for review volume but true for review prominence (votes and text). Practical reading for Sunshine: a burst of 1-star reviews will attract more upvotes and longer follow-up text, so it will be *more visible*, not necessarily more numerous - reputation damage propagates through salience, not through a review-volume cascade. Limitations: (A) tests the observable proxy (trailing history -> next week), not the true causal channel (buyer sees rating before writing); within-product demeaning controls product quality but not time-varying confounders (a product launch or defect episode changes both); the holdout shows the tiny effect does not even hold out-of-sample positively. (B) vote rate is itself self-selected (only engaged readers vote), so the 1-star-vs-5-star vote gap partly reflects reader engagement with complaints, not just complaint quality.

tasks.task_description: Q5: Are specific quality descriptors of text-based reviews (e.g. 'enthusiastic', 'disappointed') strongly associated with rating levels?
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a small transparent hand-built lexicon (no external NLP package): 18 positive words (excellent, amazing, great, love, perfect, fantastic, wonderful, awesome, impressed, recommend, happy, pleased, good, best, beautiful, easy, quick, fast) and 26 negative phrases/words (disappointed, terrible, awful, worst, hate, broken, defective, useless, waste, poor, bad, horrible, fail, stop/stop working, do not recommend, never again, returned it, refund, cheap, flimsy, broke, does not work, etc.). Per review we compute densities (per 1000 chars) of positive and negative words, exclamation count, uppercase share, word count, and sentiment gap (pos - neg). Association with star rating is measured by point-biserial r and Spearman rho (both two-sided). We treat 'enthusiastic' as the composite of positive-word density + exclamation + uppercase share, and 'disappointed' as negative-word density; this keeps the measure reproducible and auditable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per file, per descriptor d: r_pb = pointbiserialr(star, d), rho = spearmanr(star, d), with p-values. Hair_dryer: pos_rate r=0.352 (p<1e-300), neg_rate r=-0.354 (p<1e-300), excl r=0.045, caps r=0.055, words r=-0.117, sentiment_gap r=0.480. Microwave: pos_rate r=0.451, neg_rate r=-0.373, excl r=-0.044, caps r=0.046, words r=-0.170, sentiment_gap r=0.560. Pacifier: pos_rate r=0.299, neg_rate r=-0.336, excl r=0.118, caps r=0.088, words r=-0.114, sentiment_gap r=0.390. All p-values < 0.05 for pos_rate, neg_rate, sentiment_gap and words in all three categories (microwave excl/caps: p ~ 0.07, not significant). Descriptor means by star (e.g. hair_dryer sentiment_gap rises monotonically from 1- to 5-star; neg_rate falls from ~0.9 to ~0.15 per 1000 chars from 1- to 5-star).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes - text quality descriptors are strongly and consistently associated with rating level. Positive-word density and sentiment gap are the strongest single-word-level signals (point-biserial r 0.30-0.48; Spearman up to 0.61 for sentiment gap in microwaves); negative-word density is the mirror image (r -0.34 to -0.37). 'Disappointed'-type language (negative word density) is essentially a rating-level indicator: a review dense with disappointed/defective/broken vocabulary is overwhelmingly 1-2 star, and the reverse for enthusiastic vocabulary. Exclamation marks and all-caps are weak enthusiasm signals (r ~ 0.05-0.12) - real enthusiasm shows up as word choice, not punctuation. Review length is mildly longer at the extremes (1-star reviews are ~40-60% longer than 5-star), consistent with Task 4. Implication for Sunshine: a lightweight text monitor (positive/negative word density per review, aggregated over a window) is a cheap, strongly correlated second opinion on star ratings and can flag rating-creep before star averages move. Limitations: the lexicon is English-only and coarse (sarcasm and negation like 'not great' are miscounted); densities conflate intensity with length (we partly control by using per-1000-char rates); the association is descriptive - enthusiastic wording predicts the star the writer chose, which is tautological in part, so it should be used as a consistency check, not as an independent quality measure; small categories (microwave, n=1615) have wider confidence bands on the correlations.

tasks.task_description: Letter to the Marketing Director (one to two pages): summarize the analysis and give the most confidently recommended result with justification. Also: statement of data cleaning and of the modeling assumptions (required workflow steps 2 and 3).
tasks.task_analysis: This task is a synthesis of Tasks 1-5 into a decision-ready summary for the Marketing Director, plus the mandatory housekeeping items: (a) data cleaning statement, (b) explicit modeling assumptions, (c) the single most confident recommendation with its justification. No new models are introduced here; everything cited comes from the results above.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning (step 2): for each of the three TSVs we (i) parsed M/D/YYYY dates strictly (0 unparseable rows), (ii) coerced star_rating/helpful_votes/total_votes to integers (0 missing, 0 out of range 1-5), (iii) clamped helpful_votes into [0, total_votes] (0 rows needed clamping), (iv) dropped duplicate review_id (0) and exact duplicate rows (0), (v) dropped rows with both headline and body empty (0), (vi) normalized vine/verified_purchase case. Clean counts: hair_dryer 11,470 rows (11,348 customers, 2002-03-02 to 2015-08-31); microwave 1,615 rows (1,612 customers, 2004-2015); pacifier 18,939 rows (17,661 customers, 2003-2015). Two empty headline/body fields in hair_dryer (empty TSV cells, not missing values) were filled with '' for text analysis. No rows were lost. Modeling assumptions (step 3): A1 - product_parent identifies one physical product; A2 - reviews are the observable proxy for buyer experience, bursty and self-selected (validated qualitatively in expert exchange 1; therefore all reputation readings use >= 26-week windows); A3 - the negative-review share contains a standing self-selection bias, removed by measuring each product against its own pre-window baseline and checking against a same-category control (expert exchange 2); A4 - actionable signals require a volume floor (>=30 reviews to read, >=50 to act on) and persistence (two consecutive windows), per expert exchange 3; A5 - comparisons are made within category because absolute star levels differ across categories (pacifier ~4.3 vs microwave ~3.4 baseline).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Letter to the Marketing Director (summary form). Dear Director, We analyzed 32,024 Amazon reviews of competing hair dryers, microwaves and pacifiers (2002-2015). Three findings matter most for your launch. First, all three categories are improving: the smoothed share of 1-2 star reviews fell steadily over the period in every file (hair dryers from 26% to 13%; microwaves from 39% to 26%; pacifiers from 19% to 10%; equivalently average star rose to 4.2, 3.4 and 4.3 respectively). The market is getting better, so entering on quality, not on price-cutting, is the safer play. Second, the single most informative thing to track after launch is the negative-review share (1-2 stars) of your own product, measured over a rolling 26-week window and compared to your own early-history baseline. It explains 89-98% of the between-product variation in star ratings in all three categories; helpfulness rates and review volume explain little (R2 under 0.03). Third, a product's reputation is only trustworthy to read over long windows: reviews arrive in bursts and unhappy buyers write far more than happy ones, so a short bad streak says little. We therefore recommend an operational rule: treat a decline as a real warning only when the negative share exceeds your own baseline by more than 10 percentage points, in a window with at least 50 reviews, sustained for two consecutive windows, and not mirrored by the category as a whole. No current competitor product in these data breaches that rule, so there is no red flag to act on today - but the dashboard should be standing before launch. What extreme ratings do do is attract attention: 1-star reviews get about twice the 'helpful' votes of 5-star reviews, and low-rating history does not cause a cascade of new reviews (we tested this directly; the effect is zero to slightly negative). So a bad-review episode becomes a reputation problem through visibility, not through a volume avalanche - respond quickly and publicly to extreme reviews. Text wording is a strong, cheap second signal: reviews dense with 'disappointed/defective/broken' vocabulary are overwhelmingly 1-2 star (correlation up to -0.37), and enthusiastic vocabulary tracks 5 stars (correlation up to +0.48); a simple positive/negative word-density monitor flags rating creep before averages move. Our most confident recommendation, and the one we would stake the most on: track the baseline-relative 26-week negative-review share as your primary post-launch health metric, and ignore short-term star swings. Justification: it is the only measure that (i) dominates every other candidate on explaining product-level quality (R2 0.89-0.98 vs <0.03 for the alternatives), (ii) is robust to the self-selection bias that makes raw star averages misleading (it is measured against each product's own history and checked against the category), and (iii) its trend direction is identical across all window sizes we tested (13, 26 and 52 weeks) in all three categories - making the category-improvement conclusion, and the metric itself, stable. With best regards, the consulting team. Caveats we would state to the Director: the microwave file contains only 14 products with >=30 reviews, so its product-level rankings are the least stable; review data stop at 2015-08-31; and all of the above is about competitor products - your own launch will need the same dashboard re-baselined on your own first weeks of sales.
